name: ChartQA
description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 machine-generated questions over 20,882 charts curated from four online sources.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
citeAs: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning.
rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was constructed by crawling charts from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD, to ensure diversity in topics and chart styles. For the Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled because underlying data tables were not available. For the other three sources, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. The dataset includes human-authored QA pairs collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk and machine-generated QA pairs produced from human-written Statista summaries using T5 models.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consisted of publicly available chart images from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD; for three of these sources the authors also extracted underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions. Human-written chart summaries from Statista were used to generate additional QA pairs.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors extracted bounding boxes of chart elements from SVG files, extracted and structured underlying data tables, and generated additional QA pairs from human-written chart summaries using two T5 models for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation. Invalid generated questions were filtered using a heuristic that removed questions whose answers could not be found in the chart data table. The machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions. Both human-written and machine-generated QA pairs were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For Pew, only chart images were collected because data tables were unavailable. For the other sources, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions were extracted. Bounding boxes of chart elements were extracted from SVG files. For machine-generated QA pairs, T5-generated questions were filtered out if the answer could not be found in the chart data table, and the test set was manually cleaned to remove invalid questions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers were asked to focus on two types of questions for each chart image: compositional questions involving at least two mathematical or logical operations, and visual questions referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks. For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was accepted as correct; otherwise, the authors manually checked the answers to select the final correct answer. In each HIT, workers also verified two previously asked questions by other workers and provided two new QA pairs. For machine-generated annotations, two T5 models were fine-tuned on SQuAD and applied to human-written Statista summaries: one model extracted possible answers and another generated answer-aware questions.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. Because exact match does not account for typos or lexical variations, the authors manually checked 500 random samples and found agreement to be 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations. For machine-generated QA pairs, after heuristic filtering, manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart. The machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
rai:annotatorDemographics: AMT workers were selected with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5000 accomplished HITs, and were further filtered using a pretest. The paper also notes compensation based on the U.S. minimum wage and that annotations were anonymized to protect privacy.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/vis-nlp/ChartQA
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The chart sources cover topics including social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion, politics, economy, health, and society. The paper states that annotator annotations were anonymized to protect privacy.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that their models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications, and they cannot guarantee that outputs will always be correct.
rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic among all sources and particularly dominant in the Pew dataset, where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics and Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across the dataset. The machine-generated questions are derived only from Statista human-written summaries. The authors also note that previous datasets lack lexical variation, while their dataset includes informal language and typos.
rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark remains challenging because many questions involve complex visual and logical reasoning, nested operations, and informal or nuanced language. Performance drops when gold data tables are not provided, highlighting limitations of automatic chart data extraction on real-world charts with diverse styles. Pie charts and line charts are harder due to higher extraction errors. The machine-generated questions may include invalid or unanswerable items due to domain mismatch, requiring heuristic filtering and manual cleaning. The authors also note that models cannot effectively handle nested operations and that current modular extraction approaches are error-prone.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark for chart question answering with visual and logical reasoning. It provides train, validation, and test splits for both human-written (ChartQA-H) and machine-generated (ChartQA-M) QA pairs and is used for model training, validation, testing, benchmarking, transfer learning, and evaluation of chart QA systems.
